questions.q: Priya says, 'Agriculture gives 46 per cent of India's GDP, because 46 per cent of workers depend on it.' Do you agree? Explain with the two figures from the chapter.
questions.a: No. About 46 per cent is the share of workers, while the share of GDP is a little over 18 per cent. The figures measure different things: how many people depend on it, and how much value it produces.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Gives 46 per cent for workers and a little over 18 per cent for GDP
Explains that the two measure people and output, so one cannot be read as the other

questions.q: Meenakshi's family in a Tamil Nadu village grows sugarcane, keeps goats and puts bee boxes under its mango trees. How would the Government of India classify these activities together?
questions.a: The government groups crops, livestock and beekeeping as 'agriculture and allied activities'. The wrong options keep one head and drop the others, as if the broad meaning did not exist.
o: Agriculture and allied activities
Farming and horticulture only, since animals and bees are not counted
Animal husbandry only, because goats bring the main income
Forestry only, because the mango trees are the largest part

questions.q: Compare 'farming' in the narrow sense with 'agriculture and allied activities' as the government uses the term. Analyse why counting only crop growing would give a poor picture of rural livelihoods.
questions.a: Narrow farming is preparing soil and growing crops. The government's term also includes livestock, beekeeping, fisheries, silkworm rearing and silk yarn, and fibre production such as cotton and hemp. The chapter notes that in some areas farmers also rear fish or cocoons, so a family's living may come from several of these. Counting only crops would leave those out and understate how many people, about 46 per cent of workers, depend on the land.
s: Narrow sense: soil preparation and growing plants
Allied list: at least three allied activities named
Notes that farmers may combine fish or cocoon rearing with crops
Concludes the narrow count would understate dependence on agriculture

questions.q: In a survey of a rural block, a student finds that most of the people who sow, harvest and thresh are women. Which statement from the chapter does this support?
questions.a: The 75 per cent figure is the one about women. The 46 and 18 per cent figures are true but are about workers and GDP, not about who does the work. The last statement is the opposite of the book, which says women perform most operations from sowing to threshing.
o: Over 75 per cent of rural agricultural workers are women
About 46 per cent of India's working population depends on agriculture and allied activities
A little over 18 per cent of GDP comes from agriculture and allied activities
Women do only the sowing, while harvesting and threshing are men's tasks

questions.q: Out of every 1,000 workers in India in 2022-23, about how many depended on agriculture and allied activities, and what share of every ₹1,000 of the country's output did these activities supply?
questions.a: 46 per cent of 1,000 is 460 workers, and a little over 18 per cent of ₹1,000 is a little over ₹180. The wrong options swap the two figures, repeat one figure for both, or borrow the 75 per cent figure that is about women.
o: About 460 workers; just over ₹180
About 180 workers; a little over ₹460
About 460 workers; about ₹460
About 750 workers; a little over ₹180

questions.q: Differentiate between pisciculture and rearing cocoons for silk, saying what is reared in each and what is extracted in the second.
questions.a: Pisciculture is the rearing of fish. Silk rearing keeps cocoons, from which silk thread is extracted.
s: Pisciculture: fish rearing
Cocoon rearing: reared to extract silk thread

questions.q: The chapter asks, 'When you hear the word farmer, what do you visualise?' What picture does it say many people have, what does it want us to notice instead, and which figure supports it?
questions.a: Many people imagine a man. In rural India more than 75 per cent of those working in agriculture are women, who perform most operations from sowing to threshing. The figure of more than 75 per cent supports this.
s: Many imagine a man
Women do most operations from sowing to threshing
Cites more than 75 per cent

questions.q: Describe, in three or four lines, a farm family that is NOT only a crop-growing family but still comes under 'agriculture and allied activities'. Name three different activities and the broad head (farming, animal husbandry, forestry or horticulture) under which each falls.
questions.a: Any valid family, e.g. it grows paddy (farming), keeps cows (animal husbandry) and grows mango trees (horticulture). Fish rearing or silk cocoons may be added as allied activities.
s: Names three different activities
Places at least two under the correct broad head
Description is coherent and stays within the chapter's list

questions.q: A taluka has 8,000 working people. If it matched India's 2022-23 share, about ___ of them would depend on agriculture and allied activities.

'India's agricultural landscape is a blend of the traditional and the modern, with many crops and deep-rooted traditions.' Justify this using regional examples from the chapter, the economic figures and the role of women.
questions.a: Regional variety: wheat in Punjab, saffron in Kashmir, tea in the Northeast or the Nilgiris, paddy in Kerala. Economy: a little over 18 per cent of GDP and about 46 per cent of workers in 2022-23. Many families have farmed the same land for generations, which is the deep-rooted tradition. Women are more than 75 per cent of agricultural workers in rural India and do most operations.
s: Two or more regional crop examples
Both economic figures stated correctly
Link to families farming for generations
Role of women with the 75 per cent figure

questions.q: A survey team plans to interview 200 people who work in agriculture in rural India. Going by the chapter's figure for women, at least how many of the 200 should the team expect to be women?
questions.a: More than 75 per cent of rural agricultural workers are women, and 75 per cent of 200 is 150. Half (100) ignores the figure, 92 applies the 46 per cent workers share by mistake, and 36 applies the 18 per cent GDP share.
o: Above 150
About 100 women
About 92 women
About 36 women

questions.q: (a) Name the two parts of the word 'agriculture' and say what each means. (b) Rakesh says a person who only rears cattle cannot belong to agriculture, because 'agri' means field. Correct him using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Agri means field and culture means to cultivate. (b) In the broad sense agriculture covers farming, animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture, so cattle rearing belongs to it.
s: Part (a): agri is field, culture is to cultivate
Part (b): animal husbandry is included in the broad meaning of agriculture

questions.q: True or False: Because 'agri' means field, a family that only keeps bees and sells honey is outside agriculture in the sense the chapter uses.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Government of India counts beekeeping (apiculture) under 'agriculture and allied activities', so a bee-keeping family is inside agriculture in this broad sense; 'agri' describes the word's Latin origin, not the limit of the activities.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: beekeeping is listed with agriculture and allied activities; word origin does not limit the meaning

questions.q:
Assertion (A): About 46 per cent of India's working population depends on agriculture and allied activities.
Reason (R): A little over 18 per cent of India's GDP comes from agriculture and allied activities.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the 18 per cent GDP share measures value produced, not the number of workers, so it does not explain why 46 per cent of workers depend on farming.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Fig. 1.1 of the chapter shows: (i) a field ploughed with a ploughshare pulled by oxen, (ii) a farmer ploughing with a tractor, (iii) women transplanting rice seedlings by hand, (iv) seedlings transplanted with a transplanter. (a) Sort the four into traditional and modern. (b) Why does the chapter call India's agricultural landscape 'a blend' rather than one or the other?
questions.a: (a) Traditional: oxen-drawn ploughing and hand transplanting. Modern: tractor ploughing and the transplanter. (b) Both kinds are used side by side in the country, along with diverse crops and deep-rooted cultural traditions, so the landscape is a mixture.
s: Part (a): oxen ploughing and hand transplanting as traditional; tractor and transplanter as modern
Part (b): both practices exist together, so it is a blend

questions.q:
Students of Class 7 at a school in Nashik surveyed the 600 working people of Dhanori village. Crop farming: 210. Livestock rearing: 30. Beekeeping: 12. Fish farming: 8. Silk cocoon rearing: 10. Other work (shops, school, transport): 330. Of the people in the five farm-linked groups, 216 are women.
(a) Which of these entries would the government count under 'agriculture and allied activities'?
(b) What per cent of the village workers is this group, and how does it compare with the national figure in the chapter?
(c) What per cent of the farm-linked group are women, and does it fit the chapter's statement about rural India?
(d) The gram panchayat can fund only one training day: for the 210 crop growers, or for all farm-linked workers. Which would you recommend, and why?
questions.a: (a) All five farm-linked entries: crop farming, livestock, beekeeping, fish farming and silk cocoon rearing; not 'other work'. (b) 270 of 600 = 45 per cent, close to the national figure of about 46 per cent. (c) 216 of 270 = 80 per cent, which is more than 75 per cent, so it fits. (d) A defended choice: the crop-growers-only day reaches 210 of the 270 (about 78 per cent) with one focus; the wider day reaches all 270, including the allied workers and the women who are 80 per cent of the group.
s: Part (a): all five allied-inclusive entries counted, other work excluded
Part (b): 45 per cent, close to about 46 per cent nationally
Part (c): 80 per cent, above the 75 per cent in the chapter
Part (d): a recommendation supported by the figures (210 of 270 or all 270, 80 per cent women) (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: A block has 4,500 working people. If it matched the national 2022-23 share, about how many would depend on agriculture and allied activities? Show your working.
questions.a: About 46 per cent of 4,500 = 4,500 x 46 / 100 = 2,070 people.
s: Uses 46 per cent of the working population
Calculates about 2,070

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Threshing means removing the edible grain from the straw or husk, by hand or by machine.
2. Farming in India is done only by men, since women take no part in sowing, harvesting or threshing.
3. The word agriculture also takes in animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are from the chapter. 2 is false: the word 'only' is wrong, because women perform most farming operations in rural India.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Sundarpur block has 10,000 working people and produces goods and services worth ₹200 crore a year. A block officer reads in the chapter that 46 out of every 100 workers depend on agriculture and allied activities, yet these activities give only a little over 18 out of every 100 rupees of the country's output. Her colleague Imran says, 'So our farmers must be lazy.' Another colleague, Zoya, says, 'No, it only tells us how many people share a smaller part of the output.'
(a) What does each of the two figures, 46 per cent and 18 per cent, measure?
(b) If Sundarpur matched these national shares, how many of its workers and how many ₹ crore of its output would belong to agriculture and allied activities?
(c) Who reasons better from the two figures alone, Imran or Zoya? Explain in one or two lines.
(d) The block can fund only one training: beekeeping and fish rearing for farm families, or a course for crop growers only. Which fits the chapter's meaning of 'agriculture and allied activities' better, and why?
questions.a: (a) 46 per cent is the share of the working population; 18 per cent is the share of the value of goods and services produced (GDP). (b) 46 per cent of 10,000 = 4,600 workers; 18 per cent of ₹200 crore = ₹36 crore. (c) Zoya: the figures count people and output, so a large share of workers sharing a smaller share of output says nothing about laziness. (d) The allied-activities training is better supported: the chapter counts livestock, bees, fisheries and silk as part of agriculture, so many families earn from them; a crop-only course would reach only part of the group. A crop-only choice can be defended if the reason uses the stem.
s: Part (a): 46 per cent is workers, 18 per cent is GDP
Part (b): 4,600 workers and ₹36 crore
Part (c): Zoya, because the figures measure people and output, not effort
Part (d): a choice with a reason that uses the chapter's meaning of allied activities

questions.q: In a class discussion, four students decide whether a cotton and hemp fibre farm and a silk-yarn unit are covered by the Government of India's 'agriculture and allied activities'. Whose statement matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter lists fibre production such as cotton and hemp and rearing of silkworms with preparing silk yarn within the government's classification. The wrong statements each drop one or both without any support in the chapter.
o: Reena: both are listed within the government's grouping
Sunil: only the fibre crops count, since silk comes from insects
Tina: only the silk unit counts, since cotton goes to factories
Uday: neither counts, because agriculture means food grains only

questions.q: (a) A village has 300 people working in agriculture, with the share of women that the chapter gives for rural India. At least how many of them are women? (b) Why does the chapter ask 'When you hear the word farmer, what do you visualise?' and note that many people imagine a man?
questions.a: (a) More than 75 per cent of 300 = more than 225 women. (b) To show that the common picture of a farmer as a man does not match rural India, where women perform most farming operations from sowing to harvesting and threshing.
s: Part (a): more than 225
Part (b): the usual picture is a man, but women do most of the farming operations

questions.q: A museum label reads: 'Rice farming was systematically practised in the Ganga Plain in the 7th or 8th millennium BCE, because rice grains were found there.' How does the chapter treat this claim?
questions.a: The chapter reports rice grains in the Ganga Plain as early as the 7th or 8th millennium BCE, but adds that some experts say this need not mean systematic cultivation, which may have taken a few more millennia. The wrong options overclaim, deny the finding, or move it to barley.
o: Grains were found, but cultivation need not be systematic
The claim is proved, since any grain find shows systematic farming
The claim is wrong, since rice reached India only with the Harappans
The claim is right for barley, but no rice grain of that age exists

questions.q: A student draws a timeline in which the domestication of cattle (about 3500 BCE) comes after the intercropping at Kalibangan (about 2800 BCE). Show with the dates that this order cannot be right. Where would the 7th millennium BCE finds at Mehrgarh fall?
questions.a: 3500 BCE is earlier than 2800 BCE by 700 years, so domestication comes first and Kalibangan later. The Mehrgarh finds of the 7th millennium BCE are earlier than both.
s: Compares the two dates
States the gap of 700 years with the correct order
Places Mehrgarh before both

questions.q: Surapala's text says newly planted trees in arid land should be watered every morning and evening for fifteen days. A gardener who has given one tree 20 waterings on this schedule has completed ___ days.
Raghubir, a farmer in Haryana, sows mustard and wheat in alternate strips of one field in the same season. Which ancient practice from the chapter is he continuing?
questions.a: Two crops grown together in one field is intercropping, which the Kalibangan furrows show for about 2800 BCE. Grafting joins plants, seed preparation treats seeds before sowing, and domestication concerns animals.
o: Intercropping, as seen in the furrows at Kalibangan
Grafting, as described in the Brihatsamhita
Seed preparation, as given by Surapala
Domestication of animals, as in the Sindhu-Sarasvati phase

questions.q: 'Indian farming has a long and varied history.' Justify this statement using the crops, the animals and the field evidence of the chapter.
questions.a: Crops: rice in the Ganga Plain from the 7th or 8th millennium BCE; barley and millets at Mehrgarh; barley and wheat as Harappan staples. Later oilseeds, legumes, fibre crops, vegetables and fruits. Animals: cattle, sheep, goats and others domesticated from about 3500 BCE. Evidence: perpendicular furrows at Kalibangan show intercropping about 2800 BCE, and the practice continued into the 1960s.
s: Early grain crops with places
Later varieties such as oilseeds, legumes, fibre crops or fruits
Domestication of animals about 3500 BCE
Kalibangan intercropping evidence

questions.q: A horticulture teacher joins a twig of a sweet mango to a hardy plant so that the new plant is both sweet and pest-resistant. Which text does the chapter credit with describing a method of this kind that is still in use?
questions.a: The chapter says the Brihatsamhita describes a method of grafting still in use. The Vrikshayurveda is also about trees, but the book credits it with seed preparation, soil and planting advice.
o: Varahamihira's Brihatsamhita
Surapala's Vrikshayurveda
Kautilya's Arthashastra
The Krishiparashara, a text of Kautilya's time

questions.q:
Kavya's club audits her kitchen. The items are: sesame oil, black gram dal, wheat flour, a jute shopping bag, mango pickle and rice. The club wants a poster that says 'Everything in this kitchen was grown in Vedic times.' The chapter says the Vedas mention yava, godhuma, vrihi, sesame, black gram and various pulses and legumes.
(a) Name the group (oilseed, legume, fibre crop or fruit) for the sesame oil, black gram dal, jute bag and mango pickle.
(b) How many of the six items come from crops the Vedas are said to mention?
(c) Which items are missing from that list of Vedic mentions?
(d) The club has two draft posters. Draft A: 'Four of the six items in this kitchen come from crops the Vedas mention.' Draft B: 'Every item in this kitchen comes from a crop that the chapter says Indian farmers learned to grow over time.' Which draft would you print, and what must the poster not claim?
questions.a: (a) Sesame: oilseed; black gram: legume; jute: fibre crop; mango: fruit. (b) Four: sesame, black gram, wheat (godhuma) and rice (vrihi). (c) The jute bag and the mango pickle. (d) Both drafts are supported by the chapter: A is more exact about the Vedas, B covers all six items. Either can be chosen with a reason, but the poster must not say that all six items are Vedic, because the chapter does not say the Vedas mention jute or mango.
s: Part (a): oilseed, legume, fibre crop, fruit
Part (b): four of six
Part (c): jute and mango
Part (d): picks a draft with a reason and does not claim that all six items are Vedic

questions.q: Differentiate between intercropping and grafting, giving one example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: Intercropping is growing two or more different crops at the same time, e.g. sugarcane with pumpkin or the Kalibangan furrows. Grafting joins one plant with another to grow as a single plant, combining traits such as pest resistance or sweetness, e.g. the method in the Brihatsamhita.
s: Intercropping defined with an example
Grafting defined with an example

questions.q: The chapter says the old texts show 'a wealth of information about the knowledge and practices of our ancestors'. Name three kinds of information they hold and name a text for any one of them.
questions.a: Types of plants, animals, soils and climates, methods of irrigation, seed preparation, soil cultivation, planting techniques, grafting and the rearing and care of animals; for example, Surapala's Vrikshayurveda gives advice on seeds and watering.
s: Three kinds of information
One correct text matched to its information

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Rice was the first and only grain the Harappans knew.' Is he right? Answer with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Barley and wheat were the staple crops of the Harappans. Rice appears at several Harappan sites only in the 3rd millennium BCE and only in some regions, along with millets and several vegetables. So rice was neither first nor the only grain.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Barley and wheat were the staples
Rice was present only in some regions, with millets and vegetables as well

questions.q: A farmer sprinkles seeds with milk, rubs them with cow dung, dries them and smears them with honey and false black pepper before sowing. Which text in the chapter gives this advice?
questions.a: The chapter quotes this seed treatment from Surapala's Vrikshayurveda. The Brihatsamhita is credited with grafting, the Arthashastra with soaking cereals and pulses in dew, and the Vedas with naming barley, wheat and rice.
o: Surapala's Vrikshayurveda
Varahamihira's Brihatsamhita
Kautilya's Arthashastra
The Vedas

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Rice grains of the 7th or 8th millennium BCE in the Ganga Plain prove that systematic rice cultivation had already been mastered.
2. Barley and wheat were the staple crops of the Harappans.
3. Cattle, sheep, goats and other animals were domesticated from the pre-urban phase of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, about 3500 BCE.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 follow the chapter. 1 is false: the chapter says experts point out that the grains need not mean cultivation was systematic, which may have taken a few more millennia.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rice was present at several Harappan sites in the 3rd millennium BCE, at least in some regions.
Reason (R): Barley and wheat were the staple crops of the Harappans.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. The staples being barley and wheat does not explain why rice appears at some sites, so R is not the explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match the practice in Column A with the source the chapter links it to in Column B.
Column A: 1. Watering newly planted trees in arid land morning and evening for fifteen days  2. Joining two plants to combine sweetness with pest resistance  3. Soaking cereals and pulses in dew and then sun-drying them before planting  4. Growing barley and millets in the 7th millennium BCE
Column B: a. Brihatsamhita  b. Arthashastra  c. Mehrgarh  d. Vrikshayurveda
questions.a: Watering newly planted trees in arid land is from the Vrikshayurveda; grafting is from the Brihatsamhita; soaking in dew is from the Arthashastra; barley and millets in the 7th millennium BCE belong to Mehrgarh. The wrong options swap the texts that both concern seeds or trees.

questions.q: True or False: Surapala's advice to water newly planted trees morning and evening for fifteen days is meant for trees planted in every kind of soil.
questions.a: False. The chapter quotes this advice for newly planted trees in arid land; it says further recommendations give irrigation methods for other types of soils.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: the quoted advice is for arid land, and other soils have other irrigation methods

questions.q: Compare what Surapala's Vrikshayurveda and Kautilya's Arthashastra say about preparing seeds, and analyse why texts like these are valuable for understanding farming in the past.
questions.a: Vrikshayurveda: seeds sprinkled with milk, rubbed with cow dung, dried and smeared with honey and false black pepper will sprout. Arthashastra: cotton seeds smeared with cow dung; cereals, beans and pulses soaked in dew and sun-dried; sugarcane cut smeared with honey, ghee, lard and covered in cow dung. Both use cow dung. Such texts record plants, soils, climates and methods, which shows the knowledge of the ancestors in detail.
s: Vrikshayurveda seed advice
Arthashastra seed advice
Notes the common use of cow dung
Explains the value of texts as records of practice and knowledge

questions.q: Surapala advises watering newly planted trees in arid land every morning and evening for fifteen days. A school plants 12 saplings in a dry patch and follows this advice. How many times is each sapling watered, and how many waterings are done in all, counting each sapling each time?
questions.a: Twice a day for 15 days gives 30 waterings per sapling; 12 saplings x 30 = 360 waterings in all.
s: Finds 30 waterings per sapling
Finds 360 in all

questions.q:
A museum in Pune is setting up an exhibition on early farming. Three cards are ready. Card P: barley and millets at Mehrgarh, 7th millennium BCE. Card Q: cattle, sheep and goats domesticated, about 3500 BCE. Card R: perpendicular furrows in a field at Kalibangan, about 2800 BCE. One more card may be added, either on grafting in the Brihatsamhita or on Surapala's advice on watering trees.
(a) Arrange the three cards from earliest to latest.
(b) What do the perpendicular furrows on Card R show about how the Kalibangan farmers grew their crops, and what does the chapter call this practice?
(c) Besides cattle, sheep and goats, name two other animals that the chapter says were domesticated at that stage.
(d) Which fourth card would you add to show continuity with today's farming, and why?
questions.a: (a) P, Q, R. (b) Two or more different crops were grown in the same field at the same time; the practice is called intercropping, and the chapter says it continued into the 1960s. (c) Any two of asses, dogs, pigs, fowl. (d) A choice with a reason: the grafting card shows a method the chapter says is still in use today; the watering card gives detailed practical advice (fifteen days, morning and evening), but the book does not say it is still followed.
s: Part (a): P, then Q, then R
Part (b): intercropping, two or more crops at once; continued into the 1960s
Part (c): two of asses, dogs, pigs, fowl
Part (d): a choice backed by the book's statement that the grafting method is still in use, or by the detail of the watering advice (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: The chapter says barley and wheat were the staple crops of the Harappans, yet several Harappan sites also show rice in the 3rd millennium BCE, at least in some regions. (a) Which crops were the staples? (b) What does the rice find tell us about Harappan farming, and what does it not tell us?
questions.a: (a) Barley and wheat. (b) Rice was known and grown at some sites and in some regions, together with millets and several vegetables; it does not show that rice was the main or the only grain.
s: Part (a): barley and wheat
Part (b): rice was present in some regions but was not the staple grain

questions.q: A student arranges four finds from the chapter in time. Which arrangement is right?
questions.a: Rice grains in the Ganga Plain go back to the 7th or 8th millennium BCE, animal domestication to about 3500 BCE, and rice at some Harappan sites to the 3rd millennium BCE. The wrong options reverse the order.
o: Ganga Plain rice, then animal domestication about 3500 BCE, then rice at some Harappan sites
Animal domestication about 3500 BCE, then rice grains in the Ganga Plain, then rice at some Harappan sites
Rice at some Harappan sites, then rice grains in the Ganga Plain, then animal domestication about 3500 BCE
Rice at some Harappan sites, then animal domestication about 3500 BCE, then rice grains in the Ganga Plain

questions.q: (a) At which site, and around which year, does the chapter show intercropping? What in the field shows it? (b) The same practice was seen in the 1960s. Work out how many years separate 2800 BCE and 1960 CE, and say what the chapter rounds it to.
questions.a: (a) Kalibangan in Rajasthan, around 2800 BCE, shown by perpendicular furrows. (b) 2800 + 1960 = 4,760 years, which the chapter gives as around 4,800 years.
s: Part (a): Kalibangan, about 2800 BCE, perpendicular furrows
Part (b): 4,760 years, close to the chapter's 4,800

questions.q:
Lakshmi, a farmer in Andhra Pradesh, keeps a diary. Rice crop 1 is sown in June when the southwest monsoon arrives. Rice crop 2 is sown in October, when the northeast monsoon rains begin. Rice crop 3 is sown in February, a dry month. Her cousin Mohan in a north Indian village grows only the monsoon crop and leaves his field idle in the dry months.
(a) Which water source supports each of the three crops?
(b) What name does the chapter give to the water supply that makes the third crop possible?
(c) Which water sources could Mohan use in the dry months if he wanted to sow a crop?
(d) Groundwater in Lakshmi's area is falling. Should she keep the third rice crop or leave the field idle in those months? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Crop 1: southwest monsoon; crop 2: northeast monsoon; crop 3: irrigation (groundwater). (b) Irrigation. (c) Groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds or moisture retained in the soil. (d) A choice with a reason: keeping the crop uses irrigation to farm all year, as Andhra Pradesh does, but the chapter says groundwater is falling fast in many parts of India, so leaving the field idle or choosing a less thirsty crop protects the water.
s: Part (a): southwest monsoon, northeast monsoon, irrigation
Part (b): irrigation
Part (c): two dry-season sources for Mohan
Part (d): a decision tied to irrigation against falling groundwater (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: True or False: India's 15 agroclimatic zones are drawn on the basis of rainfall alone, so two regions with the same rainfall are always in the same zone.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the zones combine climate factors with types of soil and terrain and types of vegetation, so rainfall alone does not fix a zone.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: climate, soil, terrain and vegetation are combined to make the zones

questions.q: Explain how India's varied climate and its two monsoons decide what is grown, where and when. Refer to the seven climate types, the two monsoons and the 15 agroclimatic zones.
questions.a: India has seven climate types, each with different sunshine, rainfall and monsoon effects, so different crops suit different regions, as Xuanzang noticed. The southwest monsoon (June to September) is crucial for kharif crops in northern and central India. The northeast monsoon (October to December) rains on the east and south, and the Malabar and Coromandel plains get both, so the south can grow crops in between. The 15 agroclimatic zones combine climate, soil, terrain and vegetation so that agencies can plan what, when and how to grow crops.
s: Seven climate types give regional variety
Southwest monsoon: months and kharif crops
Northeast monsoon: months and regions
Coasts with both monsoons and the south growing crops in between
Agroclimatic zones for planning

questions.q: An agricultural officer must plan what, when and how to grow crops in a district by combining climate, soil, terrain and vegetation. Which scheme from the chapter helps her?
questions.a: Agroclimatic zones are made by combining climate factors, soil, terrain and vegetation. Each wrong option uses only one of these ingredients.
o: The 15 agroclimatic zones
The six major soil types alone
The three cropping seasons alone
The seven climate types alone

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh grow rice throughout the year.
Reason (R): These states get water from the monsoon as well as from irrigation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and having monsoon rain plus irrigation water is exactly what allows rice in every season, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
An agricultural officer compares two villages with invented rainfall figures. Village P: 300 mm from June to September and 450 mm from October to December. Village Q: 800 mm from June to September and no rain from October to December. One village lies on the Coromandel plain and the other in the Upper Gangetic Plain.
(a) Which village is the Coromandel one, and why?
(b) What per cent of Village P's rain falls from October to December?
(c) Which village's farmers will need more irrigation water in October to December, and from what sources can they get it?
(d) The district can give a canal-water subsidy to only one village this year. Which would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Village P: it gets a large share from the northeast monsoon (October to December), as the Coromandel plain does, while Q gets all of its rain in the southwest monsoon. (b) 450 of 750 = 60 per cent. (c) Village Q; groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds or soil moisture. (d) Two defensible answers: Q has no rain at all in its dry season, while P grows crops in between and may still need irrigation for rice in the lean months.
s: Part (a): P, because of heavy October to December rain from the northeast monsoon
Part (b): 60 per cent
Part (c): Q, with a source such as groundwater, canals, rivers or ponds
Part (d): a choice supported with the rainfall figures and the chapter's idea of a dry season (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: The chapter asks what would happen if your state received less than normal monsoon rain for two consecutive years. Describe two effects on farming and one effect on the family meal, using the chapter's ideas.
questions.a: Kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon, so they would fail or fall; farmers would need groundwater, rivers, canals or ponds; foods made from the affected crops, such as rice or pulses, could disappear from meals or become difficult to get.
s: First effect on farming
Second effect on farming or water use
An effect on food on the table, with a reason

questions.q: Differentiate between the seven climate types and the 15 agroclimatic zones.
questions.a: The seven climate types are based on climate alone (alpine, temperate, subtropical, arid, tropical wet, semi-arid, tropical). The 15 agroclimatic zones combine climate with soil, terrain and vegetation, to plan what, when and how to grow crops.
s: Climate types are classes of climate alone
Zones combine climate, soil, terrain and vegetation for farm planning

questions.q: An officer of the agriculture department must plan what, when and how to grow crops in the Upper Gangetic Plain Region. (a) What kind of division of the country is she working with, and who uses it according to the chapter? (b) Why would the seven climate types alone be a poorer basis for her plan?
questions.a: (a) She is working with the agroclimatic zones, which the government and other agencies use to plan actions to improve agricultural production. (b) The seven climate types describe climate only, while the zones also combine soil, terrain and vegetation.
s: Part (a): agroclimatic zones, used by the government and other agencies for planning
Part (b): climate types look at climate alone; the zones add soil, terrain and vegetation

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Farmers in north India depend on the northeast monsoon for their crops in the dry season between the two monsoons.
Reason (R): In that season they use groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds and moisture retained in the soil.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the northeast monsoon rains on the east and south, and the in-between period is a dry season in the north. R is true, because those are the sources the chapter names for north Indian farmers.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Joseph farms on the Malabar coast and grows crops in months when farmers in north India face a dry season. What reason does the chapter give?
questions.a: Malabar and Coromandel receive rain from both the southwest and northeast monsoons, so southern farmers can grow crops in between. The other options misstate the monsoon months, the northeast monsoon's region or the north's water sources.
o: Rain from both monsoons lets the coast grow crops in between
The southwest monsoon lasts there from June to December
The northeast monsoon rains over all of north India
North India has no water sources of any kind, so it stays dry

questions.q: Rohan says, 'India has just one rainy season, from June to September, so a farmer anywhere in India can sow only once a year.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The northeast monsoon from October to December rains on the east and south, and the Malabar and Coromandel plains get both. Southern farmers grow crops in between, and Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh grow rice throughout the year with monsoon and irrigation.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Names the second, northeast monsoon and its months and regions
Gives the all-year rice example or the crops grown in between

questions.q: A student says the Thar Desert and the western coastal strip have the same climate type. Show from the chapter's list why this cannot be right, and say what the chapter says differs between such areas.
questions.a: The Thar Desert is arid, while the western coastal strip is tropical wet, so they are different types. Each area receives different amounts of sunshine and rainfall, has different temperature changes across seasons and is affected differently by the monsoons.
s: Arid for the Thar Desert
Tropical wet for the western coastal strip
Differences in sunshine, rainfall, temperature or monsoon effect

questions.q: Compare the farming year of a farmer on the Coromandel plain with that of a farmer in the Upper Gangetic Plain, using the monsoons, and analyse why their water sources differ.
questions.a: The Coromandel plain gets rain from both the southwest and the northeast monsoons, so the farmer can grow crops in the months in between, and Tamil Nadu grows rice all year with monsoon and irrigation water. The Upper Gangetic Plain farmer depends on the southwest monsoon (June to September) for kharif crops; the in-between period is dry, so water comes from groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds and moisture in the soil. The difference arises because the northeast monsoon rains on the east and south, not on the north.
s: Coromandel: two monsoons and crops in between
Upper Gangetic Plain: depends on the southwest monsoon
Dry-season sources named
Link to where the northeast monsoon rains

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. India is divided into 15 agroclimatic zones made by combining climate, soil, terrain and vegetation.
2. The northeast monsoon, from October to December, brings rain to the east and south of India.
3. Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh can grow rice only in the monsoon months because they have no irrigation.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are from the chapter. 3 is false: those states grow rice throughout the year because of monsoon water as well as irrigation.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: (a) What did Xuanzang observe about the produce of India? (b) Which facts about India's climate in the chapter back him up?
questions.a: (a) The produce differs according to climate, soil and situation, with different flowers, plants, fruits and trees. (b) India has seven types of climate, each with different sunshine, rainfall and monsoon effects, and 15 agroclimatic zones.
s: Part (a): produce varies with climate and soil
Part (b): seven climate types or 15 zones given as support

questions.q: (a) Name the two coastal plains that receive rain from both monsoons. (b) How are their farmers better placed than those in north India in the months between the two monsoons?
questions.a: (a) The Malabar plain (Kerala) and the Coromandel plain (Tamil Nadu). (b) The rain from both monsoons lets southern farmers grow crops in between, while north Indian farmers face a dry season and must use groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds or soil moisture.
s: Part (a): Malabar and Coromandel
Part (b): crops can be grown in between in the south; the north is dry and relies on other water sources

questions.q: The southwest monsoon rains last from June to September and the northeast monsoon rains from October to December. Together the two rain-bearing monsoon periods cover ___ months of the year.
A traveller journeys from the Thar Desert to the western coastal strip and then up to the high Himalayas. Which sequence of climate types, using the chapter's list, matches her journey?
questions.a: The chapter links the Thar Desert with arid, the western coastal strip with tropical wet and the Himalayas with alpine. The wrong sequences use look-alike types such as tropical, semi-arid, temperate and subtropical.
o: Arid, tropical wet, alpine
Arid, tropical, alpine
Semi-arid, tropical wet, temperate
Subtropical, arid, alpine

questions.q: Between the two monsoons, farmers in north India face a dry season. Which of these is NOT one of the sources of water the chapter names for their crops in that season?
questions.a: The chapter names groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds and soil moisture. The northeast monsoon brings rain to the east and south of India, which is why the northern farmers are dry in that period.
o: Rain brought by the northeast monsoon
Groundwater pumped from wells and tube wells
Water from canals, rivers and ponds
Moisture retained in the soil from earlier rain

questions.q: On the Coromandel plain, Selvi sows a crop in the first week of November. Going by the chapter, which rain mainly waters it?
questions.a: The northeast monsoon prevails from October to December, and the Coromandel plain receives rain from both monsoons. The southwest monsoon brings rain from June to September, so it has ended by November.
o: The northeast monsoon, October to December
The southwest monsoon, which ends in September
No monsoon at all, as November is rainless
The southwest monsoon, which begins in November

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon.
Reason (R): The terms kharif, rabi and zaid are of Arabic origin and have been used since Mughal times.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the Arabic origin of the word says nothing about why kharif crops are sown with the monsoon, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: The chapter names two separate risks that kharif farmers face: a monsoon that arrives late, and excessive rainfall.
questions.a: True. The chapter says kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoons, and that excessive rainfall leads to the destruction of crops and distress to farmers.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: dependence on the timely monsoon, and destruction by excessive rain, are both stated

questions.q:
Match the farmer's action in Column A with the word for it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Sowing wheat in cool weather  2. Sowing rice with the first monsoon rains  3. Growing cucumber in the hot summer months  4. An older word for wet crops
Column B: a. Zaid  b. Rabi  c. Kharif  d. Kedara
questions.a: Wheat sown in cool weather is a rabi crop, rice sown with the monsoon is a kharif crop, cucumber grown in summer is a zaid crop, and kedara is the older word for wet crops. The wrong options swap the three seasons or use kedara for a season.

questions.q: In Maharashtra, Baban plans to sow bajra with the first rains, but the monsoon arrives a month late and he is worried. Which statement from the chapter explains his worry?
questions.a: Bajra is a kharif crop and the chapter says kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon. The other options give the wrong season or an absolute claim the chapter does not make.
o: Kharif crops depend on the monsoon arriving on time
Zaid crops need the monsoon to arrive before summer
Rabi crops depend on the southwest monsoon of June
Excessive rainfall is never a problem for kharif crops

questions.q: A student's revision note reads: 'Kharif crops are winter crops sown in cool weather, such as wheat and gram. Rabi crops are the monsoon crops, such as rice and maize.' Find the error in the note and write the corrected note.
questions.a: The two names are swapped. Kharif crops are the monsoon crops, such as rice and maize; rabi crops are the winter crops sown in cool weather, such as wheat and gram.
s: Finds that the two seasons are swapped
Corrects kharif: monsoon crops such as rice and maize
Corrects rabi: winter crops sown in cool weather such as wheat and gram

questions.q: Differentiate between rabi and zaid crops on the basis of season, giving two examples of each.
questions.a: Rabi crops are winter crops sown in cool weather, e.g. wheat and mustard. Zaid crops are grown in summer, e.g. watermelon and cucumber.
s: Rabi: winter season with two examples
Zaid: summer season with two examples

questions.q:
A school kitchen-garden club has 12 beds: wheat 2, maize 1, jowar 1, pumpkin 1, mustard 2, cucumber 1, gram 1, bajra 1, muskmelon 1 and peas 1. The summer vacation leaves the garden unwatered for weeks. The club now wants to give up 2 beds for a compost corner.
(a) How many beds does each cropping season hold?
(b) Which crops in the garden are affected by the unwatered summer weeks?
(c) Which season has the largest share of beds, as a fraction of all 12?
(d) From which season's beds would you take the 2 beds for compost, and why?
questions.a: (a) Kharif (maize, jowar, bajra): 3. Rabi (wheat, mustard, gram, peas): 6. Zaid (pumpkin, cucumber, muskmelon): 3. (b) The zaid crops grown in summer: pumpkin, cucumber, muskmelon. (c) Rabi: 6 of 12, which is one half. (d) The marks go to the reasoning. For example, zaid beds are at risk in the vacation and would be a natural choice, whereas taking from rabi would reduce the largest share of the garden.
s: Part (a): 3 kharif, 6 rabi, 3 zaid
Part (b): the zaid crops of summer
Part (c): rabi, half of the beds
Part (d): a choice supported by the seasons and the vacation (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: A farmer lists sugarcane, barley, muskmelon and gram. Of these, the only crop that is sown in the same cropping season as rice is ___.
questions.a: sugarcane

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Rabi crops such as wheat, barley, peas, mustard and gram are winter crops sown in cool weather.
2. Zaid crops are grown in the monsoon, so they include rice and maize.
3. Kharif crops can never be harmed by heavy rainfall, because they are monsoon crops.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is correct. 2 is false because zaid crops are summer crops such as watermelon and cucumber. 3 is false: the chapter says excessive rainfall destroys crops.
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Anita has only wheat and mustard seed in her store. Advise her. (a) In which cropping season should she sow them, and in what weather? (b) What was the older name for that season's crops? (c) Name two crops from another season that she could grow in the hot months. (d) Name two crops she could sow when the monsoon arrives, and say what could go wrong. (e) Why does the chapter value this rhythm of seasons?
questions.a: (a) Rabi, the winter season, sown in cool weather. (b) Haimana (winter crops). (c) Zaid crops, such as watermelon, cucumber, muskmelon or pumpkin. (d) Kharif crops such as rice, maize, jowar, bajra, groundnut or cotton; they depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon and excessive rain can destroy them. (e) The rhythm followed for centuries makes a wide variety of products available through the year and helps ensure the food supply.
s: Part (a): rabi, cool weather
Part (b): haimana
Part (c): two zaid crops
Part (d): two kharif crops and one risk
Part (e): variety through the year, food supply

questions.q: A cropping chart for a school garden is checked by a teacher. Which line is placed correctly under the chapter's three seasons?
questions.a: Maize and sugarcane are listed with rice, jowar and bajra as kharif crops. Peas and gram are rabi crops, cucumber is a zaid crop, and barley is a rabi crop, so the other lines each mix seasons.
o: Kharif: maize and sugarcane
Zaid: peas and gram, the summer crops
Rabi: cucumber and wheat together
Kharif: barley and bajra together

questions.q: The chapter says the rhythm of kharif, rabi and zaid is one of the factors that ensures food supply. Give two reasons why having three cropping seasons helps.
questions.a: Each season brings its own crops, so a wide variety of agricultural products becomes available throughout the year; the farmers' rhythm, followed for centuries, spreads harvests across winter, summer and the monsoon so that food is not available in only one season.
s: Variety of products reaches the people through the year
Each season has different crops
Links the rhythm to ensured food supply

questions.q: The Arthashastra says a good rainy season is one when one-third of the annual rainfall occurs at the beginning (Shravana, July-August) and at the end (Kartika, October-November) of the season, and two-thirds in the middle. (a) In which part of the season does it expect most of the rain? (b) Which cropping season's crops are sown with these rains?
questions.a: (a) In the middle of the season (August to October), where two-thirds of the rain is expected. (b) Kharif crops, the monsoon crops.
s: Part (a): the middle of the season, two-thirds of the rain
Part (b): kharif

questions.q: An old farming manual, written before the Arabic terms became common, tells farmers how to look after their haimana crops through the cool months. Which modern term does the chapter match with this?
questions.a: Haimana was the older name for winter crops, which the chapter now calls rabi. Kharif is the monsoon season, zaid is the summer season, and kedara is the older name for wet crops, not winter crops.
o: Rabi
Kharif
Zaid
Kedara

questions.q: A student labels the photograph of mustard growing in front of wheat as 'kharif', and the photograph of pearl millet as 'zaid'. (a) Correct each label. (b) Which of the two seasons you named sows its crops in cool weather with less water?
questions.a: (a) Mustard and wheat are rabi crops; pearl millet is a kharif crop. (b) The rabi season, whose crops are winter crops sown in cool weather.
s: Part (a): mustard and wheat are rabi; pearl millet is kharif
Part (b): rabi

questions.q:
A village in Madhya Pradesh grows these crops on 200 hectares. Rice 40, wheat 55, gram 25, groundnut 20, watermelon 6, cucumber 4, cotton 30, mustard 20 (hectares).
(a) Sort the crops into kharif, rabi and zaid and find the area under each season.
(b) Which season's crops are most at risk if the monsoon arrives late, and why?
(c) What fraction of the village's 200 hectares is under those crops?
(d) The panchayat can fund water support for only one group: the kharif fields or the 10 hectares of zaid crops. Which would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Kharif: rice, groundnut, cotton = 90 ha. Rabi: wheat, gram, mustard = 100 ha. Zaid: watermelon, cucumber = 10 ha. (b) Kharif crops, because they depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon. (c) 90 / 200 = 9/20 (45 per cent). (d) A choice with a reason: the kharif fields are nine times the zaid area and rely on a monsoon that is late; the zaid crops grow in summer and need water whatever the monsoon does.
s: Part (a): 90, 100 and 10 hectares correctly sorted
Part (b): kharif, because of reliance on the timely monsoon
Part (c): 9/20 or 45 per cent
Part (d): a choice that uses the hectares and the monsoon dependence (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: A student writes in a project: 'Harappan farmers divided their year into kharif, rabi and zaid and used exactly these names.' Which comment does the chapter support?
questions.a: The chapter says kharif, rabi and zaid are of Arabic origin and in use since the Mughal times; older names such as kedara, haimana and graishmika existed before. The wrong options invent earlier uses or deny the seasons themselves.
o: They are of Arabic origin, in use since Mughal times
They were used in the Vedas, and are of Sanskrit origin
They come from Sangam Tamil literature and are of Tamil origin
They were used by the Harappans, who gave them their Arabic form

questions.q: Compare kharif and rabi crops with respect to the time of sowing, examples, older names and the difficulties each faces. Then say why the chapter calls the rhythm of seasons important.
questions.a: Kharif: sown with the monsoon; rice, maize, cotton; kedara; dependent on timely monsoon and harmed by excessive rain. Rabi: winter, sown in cool weather; wheat, mustard, gram; haimana. The rhythm followed for centuries makes a wide variety of products available through the year and helps ensure food supply.
s: Sowing time of each
Examples of each
Older names of each
Kharif's dependence on monsoon timing and risk from excess rain
Importance of the rhythm for food supply

questions.q: Write a four-line riddle whose answer is 'rabi'. Use at least three facts from the chapter, such as the weather, the season and the crops.
questions.a: Any riddle using three correct facts, e.g. I am sown when the weather is cool; wheat, gram and mustard are mine; I am the winter crop season; my name came into use in Mughal times and haimana was my older name.
s: First correct fact in the riddle
Second correct fact
Third correct fact and a clear single answer 'rabi'

questions.q: Nisha grows cucumbers in her field in the hot months and then plants rice when the monsoon begins. In which order do the two crops fall in the seasons of the chapter?
questions.a: Cucumber is a zaid (summer) crop and rice is a kharif (monsoon) crop. Cucumber is not a rabi crop, and the monsoon comes after summer, not before it.
o: Zaid for the cucumber and kharif for the rice
Rabi for the cucumber and kharif for the rice
Zaid for the cucumber and rabi for the rice
Kharif for the cucumber and zaid for the rice, in that order

questions.q: A farmer's list reads: jowar, pumpkin, barley, groundnut, muskmelon, peas. Sort the six crops into kharif, rabi and zaid.
questions.a: Kharif: jowar, groundnut. Rabi: barley, peas. Zaid: pumpkin, muskmelon.
s: Kharif and rabi crops placed correctly
Zaid crops placed correctly

questions.q: Differentiate between alluvial soil and laterite soil on the basis of how each is formed and how fertile each is.
questions.a: Alluvial soil is silt deposited by rivers from the mountains and plateaus, and is rich in nutrients. Laterite soil is formed by the weathering of rock by rain, loses most minerals and is not fertile.
s: Alluvial: river silt and rich in nutrients
Laterite: weathering by rain and not fertile

questions.q: A Deccan farmer's soil formed from weathered volcanic rock, holds a lot of moisture and is very fertile. The chapter's name for this soil, which also gives it a crop-based nickname, is ___ soil.
questions.a: black

questions.q: Write three clues, in the style of 'formed from lava or old rocks; red because of iron; not very fertile', that would let a classmate identify black soil.
questions.a: Any three correct clues: formed by weathering of volcanic rocks; holds a lot of moisture; very fertile; also called cotton soil.
s: First correct clue
Second correct clue
Third correct clue, and the clues point only to black soil

questions.q: Rank any five of the six major soil types of India from the most to the least fertile. For each soil you rank, give its origin and one feature that justifies its place.
questions.a: A sample ranking (alluvial and black may be placed in either order at the top): Alluvial: silt from rivers, rich in nutrients. Black or cotton soil: weathered volcanic rock, holds a lot of moisture, very fertile. Red: weathered lava or old rocks, coloured by iron, not very fertile. Laterite or brick earth: weathering by rain, minerals washed away, hardens in heat, not fertile. Mountain or alpine: freezing and melting of ice weathers rock; thin, rough and rocky.
s: First soil with origin, feature and a sensible place
Second soil with origin, feature and a sensible place
Third soil with origin, feature and a sensible place
Fourth soil with origin, feature and a sensible place
Fifth soil with origin, feature and a sensible place; the overall order is consistent with fertility

questions.q:
The Eco Club of a school in Wardha digs a soil pit at the edge of a farm and records the layers from the bottom. Layer 1: solid rock. Layer 2: rock that is breaking into pieces. Layer 3: dark topsoil full of decayed leaves and roots, in which beans are growing. The farm owner, Mr Gaikwad, has an offer: a brick-maker will pay ₹50,000 for the top 30 cm of soil from half an acre.
(a) What is the dark organic matter in Layer 3 called, and how is it formed?
(b) What name does the chapter give to the rock of Layer 1, and what process breaks it into soil particles?
(c) How long does the chapter say soil formation takes, and why does that matter to Mr Gaikwad?
(d) Should he accept the offer? Decide and justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Humus, formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter. (b) Bedrock; weathering. (c) From a century to several millennia (the chapter also says soil forms over millions of years), so soil removed cannot be replaced within his lifetime. (d) A reasoned decision: the best supported is to refuse or limit the sale, because the topsoil with its humus gives the crops nutrients, water and support and is slow to form; accepting needs a plan to restore the soil, such as organic fertiliser.
s: Part (a): humus from decomposed plants and animals
Part (b): bedrock; weathering
Part (c): a century to several millennia; cannot be quickly replaced
Part (d): a decision that uses the nutrients and slow formation of topsoil (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: True or False: Red soil and laterite soil both owe a reddish colour to iron reacting with air and water, yet neither is fertile.
questions.a: True. The chapter says red soil is red because of iron and is not very fertile; in laterite soil most minerals are washed away leaving largely iron and aluminium, which react with air and water and give a reddish colour, and it is not fertile.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: both are reddish because of iron and both are not fertile

questions.q: (a) From what is red soil formed? (b) Why is it red, and how fertile is it?
questions.a: (a) Weathering of lava that cooled slowly, or of old rocks. (b) It contains iron, which turns reddish when it reacts with air and water; it is not very fertile.
s: Part (a): lava or old rocks
Part (b): iron gives the colour; not very fertile

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Red soil is not very fertile.
Reason (R): Red soil gets its colour from iron, which turns reddish when it reacts with air and water.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the iron that colours the soil does not explain why it is not very fertile, so R is not the explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A student on a field trip records four observations in Column A. Match each with the soil in Column B.
Column A: 1. Fine silt on a river plain, brought down from the mountains  2. Soil that turns hard in hot weather and is used as brick earth  3. Thin, rough, rocky soil on a frozen high slope  4. Dark soil that holds a lot of moisture, formed from volcanic rock
Column B: a. Laterite soil  b. Alluvial soil  c. Alpine soil  d. Black soil
questions.a: River silt is alluvial, brick earth that hardens is laterite, thin rocky soil of frozen slopes is alpine, and dark moisture-holding volcanic soil is black. The wrong options swap alluvial with black, or laterite with alluvial.

questions.q: (a) On what basis did the Amarakosha describe twelve types of agricultural land? (b) Using that same basis, name one of today's six major soil types that would rank high and one that would rank low, with the chapter's reason for each.
questions.a: (a) On soil fertility. (b) High: alluvial (rich in nutrients) or black (very fertile). Low: red or laterite (not fertile).
s: Part (a): soil fertility
Part (b): one high-ranking and one low-ranking soil, each with its fertility reason

questions.q: Compare black, red and laterite soil on how each is formed, how fertile each is and why each looks the way it does. Then say which of the three would you expect to hold the most water for a farmer who cannot irrigate, and why.
questions.a: Black: weathered volcanic rock; holds a lot of moisture; very fertile. Red: weathered lava or old rocks; red because iron reacts with air and water; not very fertile. Laterite: weathering by rain; most minerals washed away leaving iron and aluminium, which give the reddish colour; hardens in hot weather; not fertile. Black soil suits a farmer without irrigation because it holds a lot of moisture and is very fertile.
s: Formation of the three soils
Fertility of the three soils
Cause of the colour of red and laterite soil
Black soil chosen with moisture and fertility as reasons

questions.q: Along a plain, a river carries silt down from the mountains and spreads it over farmland every year. Which soil does the chapter say is formed this way?
questions.a: Alluvial soil is made of silt deposits brought by rivers from the mountains and plateaus and is rich in nutrients. Black soil comes from weathered volcanic rock, laterite from weathering by rain, and alpine soil from freezing and melting of ice.
o: Alluvial soil, from river silt
Black soil, from volcanic rock
Laterite soil, from rain weathering
Alpine soil, from freezing ice

questions.q:
A district of 20,000 hectares has four zones. Valley floor with river silt: 5,000 ha. Lava plateau with weathered volcanic rock: 8,000 ha. Old-rock uplands with reddish soil: 5,000 ha. High slopes with thin, rocky soil: 2,000 ha. The government plans to grow cotton on one zone and to bring irrigation to one other zone.
(a) Which soil type is in each zone?
(b) What per cent of the district has the fertile soils of the valley and the plateau?
(c) Which zone is best suited to cotton, and what is the soil's other name?
(d) Irrigation can be given either to the 5,000 ha of reddish soil or to the 2,000 ha of high slopes. Which will you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Valley: alluvial; plateau: black; uplands: red; slopes: alpine. (b) 13,000 / 20,000 = 65 per cent. (c) The lava plateau with black soil, also called cotton soil. (d) Any choice with a reason: red soil is not very fertile but crops can be grown on it with efficient irrigation and the area is larger; the thin, rough, rocky alpine soil would gain little and covers only 2,000 ha.
s: Part (a): alluvial, black, red, alpine
Part (b): 65 per cent
Part (c): the plateau, black or cotton soil
Part (d): a choice backed by area, fertility or the role of irrigation (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The Amarakosha describes twelve types of agricultural land based on soil fertility.
2. Humus is rich in nutrients and helps the soil retain moisture.
3. In laterite soil, most minerals are washed away, leaving largely iron and aluminium.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are in the chapter, so none of the partial combinations is correct.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: A school digs a soil pit and reads it from the bottom upward, using the chapter's diagram of how soil forms. Which order matches?
questions.a: In the diagram, solid bedrock lies at the bottom, disintegrating rock or parent material above it, and the topsoil with humus at the top. The wrong orders put the topsoil or the parent material in the wrong place.
o: Bedrock, then broken parent rock, then humus-rich topsoil
Topsoil with humus, then broken parent material, then bedrock
Broken parent material, then bedrock, then topsoil with humus
Bedrock, then topsoil with humus, then broken parent material

questions.q: A student's notebook says: 'Laterite soil: formed by silt deposited by rivers, rich in nutrients. Alluvial soil: formed when rain washes away most minerals, leaving iron and aluminium.' Find the error and write the corrected entries.
questions.a: The two descriptions are swapped. Alluvial soil is formed by silt brought by rivers from the mountains and plateaus, and is rich in nutrients. Laterite soil is formed by the weathering of rock by rain, which washes away most minerals leaving largely iron and aluminium; it is not fertile.
s: Finds that the descriptions are swapped
Corrects alluvial: river silt, rich in nutrients
Corrects laterite: rain weathering, minerals washed away, not fertile

questions.q: A farmer spreads rotted crop residue and dung on a worn-out field every year. After some years the soil is darker and stays moist longer. Which substance has built up, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Humus is dark organic matter formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter; it is rich in nutrients and retains moisture. Silt is river-borne sediment, bedrock is the original rock, and weathered lava gives red soil.
o: Humus, from decayed plant and animal matter
Silt, which rivers carry down from the mountains
Bedrock, the original rock that soils come from
Weathered lava, which turns reddish with iron

questions.q: On a hill in Kerala, Meera sees a soil that goes hard in hot weather, is used for bricks, has lost most of its minerals to rain and is left with iron and aluminium. Which soil is it?
questions.a: Hard in hot weather, brick earth, minerals washed away by rain and mostly iron and aluminium describe laterite soil. Red soil is also reddish and infertile but does not harden or lose minerals in this way.
o: Laterite
Red soil from old rocks
Alluvial soil from river silt
Black soil from volcanic rock

questions.q: On a field trip to the Deccan, Pooja finds a dark soil formed from weathered volcanic rocks that holds a lot of moisture and is very fertile. Which soil is it?
questions.a: Weathered volcanic rock, high moisture and high fertility describe black soil. Red soil also comes from lava or old rocks but is not very fertile; alluvial soil is river silt; laterite is washed free of minerals by rain.
o: Black soil
Red soil
Alluvial soil
Laterite soil

questions.q: (a) What makes silt easy for rivers to carry from the mountains to the plains, according to the chapter's description of it? (b) How does this help explain why alluvial soil is found on river plains?
questions.a: (a) Silt is fine-grained, dust-like sediment of rock and mineral particles larger than clay but smaller than sand, so it is easily transported by rivers. (b) Rivers carry silt from the mountains and plateaus and deposit it on the plains, where it forms alluvial soil.
s: Part (a): silt is fine, dust-like, larger than clay and smaller than sand, so rivers transport it easily
Part (b): rivers deposit the silt on the plains and it forms alluvial soil

questions.q: In the book's figure of crops grown in different soil areas, a note says that crops marked with an asterisk are not on the ideal soil for their cultivation but can be grown with efficient irrigation. What does this show about the link between soil and crops, and what can make up for a less ideal soil?
questions.a: Soil strongly influences which crops thrive, which is why most crops are shown on their ideal soils. Efficient irrigation can make up for a less ideal soil.
s: Soil strongly influences which crops grow well
Efficient irrigation can make up for a less ideal soil
Links the two: the starred crops are possible on less ideal soil only because of irrigation

questions.q: Savita sows maize, a pulse and a vegetable in different parts of one field so that something is ready to harvest every few months. (a) Which method of the chapter is this? (b) Give two benefits the chapter mentions, and say how this method differs from crop rotation.
questions.a: (a) Multiple cropping. (b) It reduces the risk of pests and ensures at least one crop. It differs from crop rotation, which grows different crops in the same field in different seasons to stop the soil losing specific nutrients, while multiple cropping grows several crops in the same field.
s: Part (a): multiple cropping
Part (b): two benefits (fewer pests, at least one crop) and the contrast with rotation

questions.q: Compare traditional irrigation systems (the phad system and bamboo drip irrigation) with modern ones (drip and sprinkler). Then analyse why the chapter says modern methods are important today.
questions.a: Phad: community-based, small canals divert river water to fields in Maharashtra. Bamboo drip: bamboo pipes channel spring water to fields in the northeast. Drip: tubes and emitters deliver water slowly to the roots. Sprinkler: sprays water into the air like artificial rain. Modern methods use water more efficiently, which is necessary as groundwater is fast decreasing, and they allow farming in low-rainfall areas.
s: Phad system described
Bamboo drip described
Drip and sprinkler described
Groundwater is decreasing so efficiency is needed
Another gain such as farming in low rainfall or stable food supply

questions.q: On a hill farm, Ravi ploughs along the natural curves of the slope so that rainwater does not wash his soil away. Which method is he using?
questions.a: Ploughing along the natural curves of a slope is contour ploughing. Terracing cuts flat steps, rotation changes crops and mulching covers the soil.
o: Contour ploughing
Crop rotation, changing the crop
Terracing, cutting flat steps
Mulching, covering the soil

questions.q: Banana trees are planted on the bunds of a farmer's paddy fields. Which of these is NOT a benefit the chapter gives for them?
questions.a: The chapter says such banana trees serve as windbreakers, hold the soil in place and provide another crop. It does not say they replace irrigation.
o: They remove the need to irrigate
They act as windbreakers for the paddy field
They hold the soil in place on the bunds
They give the farmer another crop to sell

questions.q: A farmer wants water delivered slowly and directly to the plant roots through a network of tubes and emitters. The method she should use is called ___ irrigation.
questions.a: drip

questions.q: True or False: Healthy soil is only a store of minerals, and living things such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms do not matter for the plants growing in it.
questions.a: False. The chapter calls soil a complex ecosystem; organisms like bacteria, fungi, earthworms and insects break down organic material and improve the health of the soil, enabling it to sustain healthy plants.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: soil organisms break down organic material and keep the soil healthy for plants

questions.q: Ishita says, 'Panchagavya is only an old belief and has no proven benefit.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. Panchagavya is a fermented mixture of dung, urine, milk, curd and ghee, and recent studies have shown that it acts as a biofertiliser, enhancing crop growth and productivity and increasing resistance to disease.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Names what panchagavya is
Recent studies show biofertiliser effect and higher productivity or disease resistance

questions.q: A farmer's hill field is losing soil to rainwater, and her crops have taken the same nutrients from it year after year. Advise her. Choose four methods from the chapter, say which problem each one solves and how, and explain why the chapter treats healthy soil as crucial.
questions.a: Healthy soil is a complex ecosystem and crucial for a good harvest. Crop rotation: different crops in different seasons so the soil does not lose specific nutrients. Contour ploughing: ploughing along the curves of the slope to avoid erosion by rainwater. Terracing: flat steps slow down water runoff. Organic fertilisers like cow dung replenish nutrients. Afforestation, mulching and ploughing back crop residue are also named.
s: Healthy soil matters: a living ecosystem crucial for a good harvest
First method matched to its problem
Second method matched to its problem
Third method matched to its problem
Fourth method matched to its problem

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Rain-fed farming relies entirely on rainfall, so droughts and unpredictable monsoons are no problem for it.
2. Contour ploughing means ploughing along the natural curves of a hill slope to avoid soil erosion from rainwater.
3. Sprinkler irrigation delivers water slowly and directly to the roots through tubes and emitters.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 2 is correct. 1 is false: farmers who depend on rain face droughts and unpredictable monsoons. 3 describes drip irrigation, while sprinklers spray water like artificial rain.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Which pair below contains one traditional and one modern irrigation system from the chapter?
questions.a: The phad system is traditional and sprinkler irrigation is modern. Drip and trickle irrigation are one and the same modern method, the phad system and bamboo drip are both traditional, and sprinkler and drip are both modern.
o: Phad system and sprinkler irrigation
Drip irrigation and trickle irrigation
Phad system and bamboo drip irrigation
Sprinkler irrigation and drip irrigation

questions.q: The chapter calls efficient modern irrigation 'very necessary'. Give the reason and two benefits irrigation has brought.
questions.a: Groundwater reserves are fast decreasing in many parts of India, so water must be used efficiently. Irrigation enables farming even in areas of low rainfall, increases crop yields and ensures a more stable food supply.
s: Reason: groundwater is fast decreasing
First benefit
Second benefit

questions.q:
Chandrakala farms 3 hectares in a low-rainfall village of Marathwada. She has no canal or well, only a small pond that collects rainwater. For the dry months she can fit either a drip set at ₹60,000 per hectare or a sprinkler set at ₹25,000 per hectare. She has ₹1,20,000 to spend.
(a) Is her farming rain-fed or irrigated, and what does the chapter say a small pond does for the soil?
(b) How does drip irrigation deliver water, and how do sprinklers differ?
(c) How many hectares can she cover with ₹1,20,000 under each choice, up to her 3 hectares?
(d) Which would you advise her to buy, and why?
questions.a: (a) Rain-fed; a small pond collects rainwater and provides moisture to the soil for a longer period. (b) Drip delivers water slowly and directly to the roots through tubes and emitters; sprinklers spray water into the air, to fall like artificial rain. (c) Drip: 1,20,000 / 60,000 = 2 hectares. Sprinkler: all 3 hectares, costing ₹75,000. (d) A defended choice: drip uses water most efficiently at the roots but covers only 2 of her 3 hectares; sprinklers cover all 3 hectares and leave ₹45,000, but water is sprayed over the whole crop.
s: Part (a): rain-fed; the pond keeps moisture in the soil longer
Part (b): drip at the roots; sprinklers like rain
Part (c): 2 hectares and 3 hectares
Part (d): a choice that weighs area covered against water efficiency (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: A farmer's field lies on a hill slope. Name two measures from the chapter that reduce soil erosion there and say how each works.
questions.a: Any two of: terracing - flat steps slow down water runoff; afforestation - planted trees help prevent erosion; contour ploughing - ploughing along the curves prevents rainwater from washing the soil.
s: First measure with its working
Second measure with its working

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In many parts of India, groundwater reserves are fast decreasing.
Reason (R): Drip and sprinkler irrigation help to use water more efficiently.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but efficient irrigation is a response to falling groundwater, not the cause of it, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Write a short situation (three or four lines) in which a farmer would prefer irrigated farming to rain-fed farming. Then name one traditional structure or system and one modern method she could use.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. a farmer in a dry area with an unpredictable monsoon. Traditional: any of kull, kund, ahar, pokhar, khadin, arakere, eri, phad, bamboo drip, farm ponds or Kallanai-type structures. Modern: drip or sprinkler irrigation.
s: Situation that justifies irrigation
One traditional system named
One modern method named

questions.q: Sunita grows maize in the kharif season and a pulse crop in the rabi season on the same field, so that the soil does not keep losing the same nutrients. Which method of the chapter is she using?
questions.a: Growing different crops in the same field in different seasons so the soil does not lose specific nutrients is crop rotation. Multiple cropping grows several crops in a field together, contour ploughing follows slope curves, and afforestation plants trees.
o: Crop rotation
Multiple cropping
Contour ploughing
Afforestation

questions.q:
Match the water source or delivery in Column A with the irrigation method of the chapter in Column B.
Column A: 1. Small canals divert river water to fields, run by the community  2. Bamboo pipes bring spring water to fields  3. Tubes and emitters release water slowly at the roots  4. Water is sprayed into the air and falls like artificial rain
Column B: a. Sprinkler irrigation  b. Phad system  c. Drip irrigation  d. Bamboo drip irrigation
questions.a: Canals from a river run by the community are the phad system, bamboo pipes from springs are bamboo drip irrigation, tubes and emitters at the roots are drip irrigation, and spraying like rain is sprinkler irrigation. The wrong options swap two methods.

questions.q: (a) Who built Kallanai, across which river, and about how long ago does the chapter place it? (b) Taking the present year as 2026 CE and the Munsar Lake as an 11th-century CE work of Queen Minaldevi, which is older, and by about how many years?
questions.a: (a) Karikala built it across the Kaveri about 1,800 years ago, around 226 CE. (b) Kallanai is older: the 11th century CE is 1001-1100 CE, so the gap is about 775 to 875 years, roughly 800.
