s: Part (a): Karikala, Kaveri, about 1,800 years ago (around 226 CE)
Part (b): Kallanai older, by roughly 800 years

questions.q:
Devraj has 5 hectares on a hill in Uttarakhand. The soil lost each year, in tonnes per hectare, is 24 when he ploughs up and down the slope, 12 when he ploughs along the natural curves of the slope, and 4 when he cuts flat steps into the hillside. Ploughing along the curves costs nothing extra. Cutting steps costs ₹80,000 per hectare, and he can spend ₹2 lakh.
(a) Name the method that ploughs along the curves and the method that cuts steps, and say what the second does to water runoff.
(b) By what per cent does ploughing along the curves cut soil loss compared with ploughing up and down?
(c) How much soil is lost a year if all 5 hectares are ploughed along the curves, and if 2.5 hectares get steps and 2.5 are ploughed along the curves?
(d) Is cutting the steps worth ₹2 lakh? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Contour ploughing; terracing creates flat steps that slow down water runoff and reduce soil erosion. (b) (24 - 12) / 24 = 50 per cent. (c) All contour: 5 x 12 = 60 tonnes. Mixed: 2.5 x 4 + 2.5 x 12 = 40 tonnes. (d) Whichever is chosen needs a reason: spending ₹2 lakh cuts annual loss by 20 more tonnes (60 to 40) and protects soil that takes millions of years to form; or the free contour method already halves the loss, so the money could go elsewhere.
s: Part (a): contour ploughing; terracing makes flat steps that slow runoff
Part (b): 50 per cent
Part (c): 60 tonnes and 40 tonnes
Part (d): a decision using the extra 20 tonnes saved and the cost (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: A student says the photograph of Munsar Lake at Viramgam shows that people in India have regarded water bodies as sacred. Which detail given with the photograph supports her?
questions.a: The chapter points to the shrines and temples on its banks as a reminder that water bodies are regarded as sacred. The queen, the date and the artificial origin do not speak of sacredness, and the canals belong to the phad system.
o: Its banks have small shrines and some temples
It was built by a queen in the 11th century CE
Like many city lakes in India, it is artificial
It sends river water to fields by small canals

questions.q: Differentiate between rain-fed and irrigated agriculture, and state one challenge faced in rain-fed farming.
questions.a: Rain-fed agriculture relies entirely on rainfall; irrigated agriculture supplies water to crops by artificial methods. A challenge of rain-fed farming is drought or an unpredictable monsoon.
s: Rain-fed and irrigated correctly distinguished
One challenge of rain-fed farming

questions.q: Before the seed drill, a farmer did soil preparation, seed planting and closing the furrow as three separate steps on each of 5 plots. Using a seed drill, each plot needs one operation, so the number of separate steps saved in all is ___.
A farmer says, 'Machines that save labour in sowing came only with the Green Revolution.' (a) Which three operations did the ancient Indian seed drill combine into one? (b) Use this to correct him.
questions.a: (a) Soil preparation, seed planting and closing the furrow. (b) The seed drill is an ancient invention of Indian farmers that cut a three-step operation to one, so labour-saving sowing equipment is much older than the Green Revolution.
s: Part (a): soil preparation, seed planting and closing the furrow
Part (b): the seed drill is an ancient Indian invention, so he is wrong

questions.q:
A farmer compares two plots of one hectare, with grain priced at ₹20,000 per tonne. The chemical plot gives 5.0 tonnes in year 1 and 4.4 tonnes in year 5, with inputs costing ₹30,000 a year. The organic plot (compost and neem-based sprays) gives 3.8 tonnes in year 1 and 4.3 tonnes in year 5, with inputs costing ₹12,000 a year. The farmer has a loan to repay this year.
(a) Which plot follows the Green Revolution method, and name two of its inputs.
(b) Find the net income of each plot in year 1.
(c) Find the net income of each plot in year 5.
(d) Which plot should the farmer prefer? Decide and justify with the numbers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The chemical plot; high-yielding seed, fertilisers or pesticides. (b) Chemical: 5.0 x 20,000 - 30,000 = ₹70,000. Organic: 3.8 x 20,000 - 12,000 = ₹64,000. (c) Chemical: 4.4 x 20,000 - 30,000 = ₹58,000. Organic: 4.3 x 20,000 - 12,000 = ₹74,000. (d) A choice with reasons: chemical gives ₹6,000 more in year 1 for the loan, but yields fall as the soil is impoverished, and organic pulls ahead by year 5.
s: Part (a): chemical plot, two Green Revolution inputs
Part (d): decision balancing the loan against long-term soil health (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: Harpreet bought high-yielding seeds from a company, but the seeds from his own harvest sprouted poorly the next year, so he must buy again. Which concern of the chapter does this show?
questions.a: The chapter says seeds from company plants are often unsuitable for the next season, creating dependency. The other options are false or unrelated claims.
o: Farmers become dependent on seed companies
Company seeds always give a lower yield than old seeds
Company seeds are never pest-resistant
Seeds cannot be shared in families or communities

questions.q:
Match the farmer's practice in Column A with its name in Column B.
Column A: 1. Cows give manure for the fields and bullocks plough them  2. A Konkan family grows food crops, spices and medicinal plants around its home  3. Steps are cut into a hillside to make flat land  4. Seeds are coated with a paste of cow dung and urine before planting
Column B: a. Terrace farming  b. Beejamrit  c. Gokrishi  d. Kulagar
questions.a: Cows for manure and bullocks for ploughing is gokrishi, a homestead garden in the Konkan is kulagar, steps cut into hillsides are terrace farming, and a seed-coating paste of cow dung and urine is beejamrit. The wrong options swap the two household systems or the two soil-and-seed practices.

questions.q: True or False: Coating seeds with beejamrit before planting protects them from being spoilt and also shortens the time they take to germinate.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the ICAR-developed paste of cow dung and urine, combined with other materials, protects the seeds from being spoilt and reduces germination time.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: the chapter gives both effects, protection from spoilage and shorter germination time

questions.q: A farmer wants to cut down on chemical sprays and fertilisers. Suggest two options from the chapter's sustainable pathways.
questions.a: Any two of organic farming with natural fertilisers (compost, seed cake, animal manure), neem-based pesticides, and the traditional methods that ICAR found valid.
s: First option
Second option

questions.q: Dev says, 'The Green Revolution was a complete success, so nobody questions that kind of farming now.' Is he fully right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Only partly. It increased food grain production, especially of wheat and rice, and India became self-sufficient in food. But its limits have become visible: long-term impoverishment of soil, depletion of groundwater, contamination by pesticides and fertilisers and damage to health, so more and more agricultural scientists question its sustainability.
s: Verdict: partly right, not completely
Credits the gains: more wheat and rice, self-sufficiency in food
Gives the limits and notes that scientists question its sustainability

questions.q:
Two neighbours, Mehar and Sonu, each farm 3 hectares. Mehar saves seed from her own crop: it yields 30 quintals per hectare and the seed costs ₹1,500 per hectare. Sonu buys company seed every year: it yields 36 quintals per hectare and costs ₹6,000 per hectare. Wheat sells at ₹2,200 per quintal.
(a) Whose seed choice creates dependence on companies, and why?
(b) Find each farmer's income per hectare after deducting the seed cost.
(c) How much more does Sonu earn on 3 hectares?
(d) Mehar is thinking of switching to company seed. What should she weigh before deciding?
questions.a: (a) Sonu's: company seeds are often unsuitable for replanting, so he must buy again. (b) Mehar: 30 x 2,200 - 1,500 = ₹64,500. Sonu: 36 x 2,200 - 6,000 = ₹73,200. (c) 8,700 x 3 = ₹26,100. (d) A choice with reasons: the extra ₹8,700 per hectare against the yearly dependence on the company and the recurring seed cost; she could also coat her own seed with beejamrit.
s: Part (a): Sonu, since company seed is often not suitable for replanting
Part (d): weighs the extra income against dependence (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Green Revolution made India self-sufficient in food grains.
Reason (R): It introduced high-yielding seeds, more irrigation, chemical fertilisers and pesticides, and mechanised equipment.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and these inputs raised wheat and rice production, which gave self-sufficiency, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Gokul's family in a Konkan village of Goa grows food crops, spices, fruit and medicinal plants around their house in a structured, irrigated design. Which traditional system is this?
questions.a: Kulagar is the Konkan homestead system. Gokrishi uses cows for manure and bullocks for ploughing, and terrace farming cuts steps on slopes.
o: Kulagar
Gokrishi
Terrace farming
The Sikkim organic model

questions.q: State one advantage and one drawback of buying seeds from companies, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Advantage: higher yields and pest resistance. Drawback: the seeds the plant later produces are often unsuitable for planting in the next season, creating dependency on the seed companies.
s: One advantage
One drawback

questions.q: Compare traditional farming and Green Revolution farming on productivity and long-term effects, as the chapter does.
questions.a: Green Revolution methods are highly productive and produce a large amount of food quickly, but harm the soil, pollute water and harm creatures like bees. Traditional methods work in harmony with nature and are more resilient and sustainable, but may yield less.
s: Productivity of modern methods
Harmful long-term effects of modern methods
Traditional methods: resilient and sustainable but possibly lower yield

questions.q: A district's wheat and rice output rises sharply after farmers adopt high-yielding seeds, more irrigation, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and machines. (a) Name the movement of the 1960s and 1970s that introduced these. (b) Name two long-term problems the chapter says its approach has shown.
questions.a: (a) The Green Revolution. (b) Any two of: long-term impoverishment of the soil, depletion of groundwater, contamination of soil and water by pesticides and fertilisers, damage to human and animal health.
s: Part (a): the Green Revolution
Part (b): two long-term problems from the chapter

questions.q: In one village, yields keep falling and the water table keeps dropping, even though farmers use more fertiliser and pump more groundwater each year. Which explanation fits the chapter's view of the Green Revolution approach?
questions.a: The chapter says the limits of the Green Revolution have become visible over the last few decades, including long-term impoverishment of the soil and depletion of groundwater. It also says production of wheat and rice rose significantly, so the other explanations contradict it.
o: Its limits appear over decades: poorer soil, falling groundwater
Its methods fail at once, as they never raise wheat or rice output
Its seeds resist pests, so any loss is the weather's doing
Its machines cannot be used on any farm, so yields must fall

questions.q: A speaker says, 'Traditional farming has nothing scientific in it, so modern science has nothing to learn from it.' Show from the chapter why this cannot be right. (The chapter reports that ICAR documented almost 5000 traditional practices and that over 85 per cent of these practices were validated by modern science.)
questions.a: The chapter reports that over 85 per cent of the practices were validated by modern science and could be applied to reduce chemical use and improve soil health. Neem-based pesticides and beejamrit show traditional ideas turned into modern solutions.
s: Cites the ICAR validation
Says they can reduce chemicals and improve soil health
Gives an example such as neem-based pesticides or beejamrit

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient-rich water solutions, giving the essential minerals directly to the roots.
2. Seeds from company-developed plants can always be sown again in the next season.
3. Sikkim, called the world's first 100 per cent organic state, banned chemical fertilisers and pesticides in 2014.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are from the chapter. 2 is false: 'always' is wrong, because the seeds are often not suitable for planting in the next season.
o: 1 and 3 only
3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: The word kulagar comes from the Konkani 'kula' and 'agar'. (a) What do the two parts mean? (b) How does a Konkan family's garden of food crops, spices, fruit and medicinal plants around its home fit the meaning of the whole word?
questions.a: (a) Kula means family and agar means storehouse. (b) The family's own home garden acts as a storehouse of many crops for the family, in a structured irrigated design around the house.
s: Part (a): kula is family and agar is storehouse
Part (b): the household garden is the family's storehouse of varied produce

questions.q: 'Sustainable agriculture combines the productivity of modern methods with the wisdom of traditional practices.' Justify this using the gains and limits of the Green Revolution, the strengths of traditional systems and two examples of sustainable pathways.
questions.a: Green Revolution: HYV seeds, irrigation, chemicals and machinery made India self-sufficient in food, but caused soil impoverishment, groundwater depletion and contamination. Traditional farming treats soil and plant as one system and works with nature, but may yield less. Sustainable pathways combine the two: organic farming with compost, seed cake and manure, and neem-based pesticides. Sikkim became 100 per cent organic in 2014.
s: Gains of the Green Revolution
Limits of the Green Revolution
Strengths and weakness of traditional systems
Two examples of sustainable pathways
Concluding link: balance of the two

questions.q: Compare terrace farming, kulagar and gokrishi. Analyse why the chapter treats them as examples of traditional systems that see the plant and soil as one complete system.
questions.a: Terrace farming: steps cut into a hillside to give flat land, preventing erosion and conserving water. Kulagar: a homestead system in the Konkan with varied crops around the home in a structured irrigated design. Gokrishi: cows provide manure and bullocks plough. All work with the natural cycle and farmyard resources: the soil supplies nutrients, soil organisms convert them for plants, and plants feed the organisms through their roots.
s: Terrace farming described
Kulagar described
Gokrishi described
Soil, organisms and plants as one system

questions.q: After Sikkim's 2014 ban on chemical fertilisers and pesticides, a Sikkim farmer wants to protect his crop from insects in a way that fits the chapter's sustainable pathways. What should he use?
questions.a: Neem-based pesticides are natural and much less harmful to the environment, which suits organic farming. Chemical pesticides and fertilisers are what the ban removed, and a seed variety alone does not protect against insects.
o: A neem-based pesticide
A chemical pesticide
A chemical fertiliser
A high-yielding seed alone

questions.q: Ananya lives in a city flat with no garden or soil and wants to grow salad vegetables indoors in a controlled setting. Which method from the chapter suits her?
questions.a: Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient-rich water solutions in controlled environments, so it suits urban farming and poor soil. Terracing and contour ploughing need a hill slope, and rain-fed farming needs open land and rainfall.
o: Hydroponics, growing plants in nutrient-rich water
Terracing, cutting flat steps into a hillside for growing
Contour ploughing along a slope to stop erosion
Rain-fed farming on open land that depends on rainfall

questions.q: Untimely heavy rain has destroyed Ramesh's standing crop, and he wants financial assistance for the loss. Which government support from the chapter is meant for this?
questions.a: Crop insurance such as the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana gives financial assistance against crop loss. Cheaper electricity lowers input costs, purchase of crops helps marketing, and forecasts help planning.
o: Crop insurance, such as Fasal Bima Yojana
Electricity for irrigation at lower prices for farmers
Purchase of important crops at fair prices from them
Weather forecast information for farmers' planning

questions.q:
Sarita farms 2 hectares of paddy. Cultivation costs ₹40,000 per hectare and the expected crop is worth ₹90,000 per hectare. Untimely heavy rain destroys 60 per cent of the crop. She had insured the crop under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana at a premium of ₹5,000 for the 2 hectares. Assume the scheme pays out ₹40,000 for such a loss.
(a) Why does a farmer like Sarita need such a scheme?
(b) What was the value of the crop destroyed?
(c) What is her net result, with and without insurance, after cultivation costs?
(d) A neighbour says the ₹5,000 premium is wasted in a good year, when the crop would earn her ₹1,00,000 after costs, so he will rely on a loan. Whose choice is wiser for a farmer like Sarita? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Untimely or extreme weather can destroy crops and cause heavy losses, and crop insurance gives financial assistance. (b) 60 per cent of ₹1,80,000 = ₹1,08,000. (c) Without insurance: 72,000 - 80,000 = -₹8,000. With insurance: -8,000 + 40,000 - 5,000 = ₹27,000. (d) A defended choice: insured, she turns a loss of ₹8,000 into a gain of ₹27,000 and avoids a loan that could lead to a debt trap; the neighbour saves ₹5,000 in good years and is acceptable only if he can bear a loss like this one.
s: Part (a): weather can destroy crops; insurance gives financial assistance
Part (c): -₹8,000 without and ₹27,000 with insurance
Part (d): a decision weighing the premium against the loss and the debt trap (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: A farm measures 25,000 square metres. Taking 1 hectare as 10,000 square metres, the farm is ___ hectares.

(a) According to some estimates, how many farmers a day are compelled to abandon agriculture? (b) What does the chapter give as the path that leads to this, and how many farmers would that be in a week at this rate?
questions.a: (a) As many as 2,300 every day. (b) Loans taken in times of hardship that are difficult to repay, catching farmers in a debt trap; 2,300 x 7 = 16,100 farmers a week.
s: Part (a): 2,300 a day
Part (b): hardship loans and the debt trap; 16,100 in a week

questions.q: True or False: According to the chapter, the traditional extra incomes of farming families, such as cows, goats, poultry and fishing, are now enough to give farmers a decent quality of life.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that diversity builds resilience and families traditionally have such income, but today this is proving to be inadequate to provide a decent quality of life to farmers.

questions.a: (a) 'Diversity builds resilience': other sources of income keep the family going when the crop is hit. (b) Today these sources are proving inadequate to provide a decent quality of life to farmers.

questions.q: A farmer says, 'The government helps only at the end, by buying crops after harvest.' (a) Name two kinds of government help from the chapter that reach farmers before harvest. (b) Name one that helps at or after harvest.
questions.a: (a) Any two of seeds, fertilisers and pesticides; weather forecast information; research and training; electricity for irrigation at lower prices; crop insurance. (b) Any one of purchase of important crops at fair prices, cold storages, digital access to information and markets.
s: Part (a): two forms of help before harvest, such as seeds, forecasts, training or cheaper electricity
Part (b): one form of help at or after harvest, such as purchase of crops or cold storage

questions.q: A village has a good wheat harvest, but traders offer very low prices. Which help from the chapter is meant to ensure that farmers have no difficulty marketing their produce and get fair prices?
questions.a: The chapter says the government purchases important crops from farmers so that they face no difficulty marketing their produce and get fair prices. Seeds, forecasts and training help before the harvest, not the sale.

The government supplying seeds and fertilisers
The government giving weather forecasts
The government providing training on new practices

questions.q: Mohan has 0.75 hectare and is advised to buy a large tractor. (a) Give two reasons from the chapter why this is a poor fit for him. (b) What recent change might still help him?
questions.a: (a) Machines are designed for larger farms, and they are expensive to buy or rent. (b) Of late, machines have also been designed and invented for small farms.
s: Part (a): designed for larger farms and expensive to buy or rent
Part (b): machines have recently been designed for small farms

questions.q: Four brothers inherit 3 hectares and divide it equally. How does each brother's share compare with the average landholding given in the chapter?
questions.a: 3 hectares among four is three-fourths of a hectare each, which is the average landholding in the chapter. Half, one and a half or double come from not dividing correctly.

It is half of it

It is double it

questions.q:
Thakur's family had 6 hectares. His three sons divided it equally. One son, Arun, later divided his share equally between his two children. A hectare of crops gives about ₹60,000 net a year. Arun's daughter Meenu keeps 15 goats and some poultry, earning ₹25,000 and ₹15,000 a year. A machine designed for small farms costs ₹1.2 lakh; it would save her about ₹12,000 a year in labour, and she could rent it to neighbours for about ₹18,000 a year.
(a) How many hectares does Arun get, and how many does Meenu get?
(b) Is Meenu's holding above or below the national average, and by how much?
(c) What are Meenu's yearly earnings from crops and from other sources together, and what share of this is from other sources?
(d) Meenu is thinking of buying the machine. Advise her.
questions.a: (a) Arun: 6 / 3 = 2 hectares. Meenu: 2 / 2 = 1 hectare. (b) Above the average of three-fourths of a hectare by one-fourth of a hectare. (c) Crops ₹60,000 plus other sources ₹40,000 = ₹1,00,000; other sources are 40 per cent. (d) A reasoned decision: buying brings about ₹30,000 a year, so it pays back in about 4 years, and the chapter says machines for small farms now exist; but ₹1.2 lakh is more than a year of her total earnings and may mean a loan, which the chapter links to the debt trap. Renting a machine or adding more livestock income are alternatives.
s: Part (a): 2 hectares and 1 hectare
Part (b): above, by one-fourth of a hectare
Part (c): ₹1,00,000 with 40 per cent from other sources
Part (d): advice that weighs the machine's cost and payback against the loan risk (the reason must use a figure or fact from the stem)

questions.q: A newspaper says, 'Dividing land among heirs does no harm, because each heir gets the same farm as the father.' A farmer has 3 hectares; he divides it equally among four children, and each of them later divides her share equally among three children. Show that the claim cannot be right and find the final holding in square metres.
questions.a: Each child gets 3 / 4 = 0.75 hectare, and each grandchild gets 0.75 / 3 = 0.25 hectare, which is 2,500 square metres. The holding shrinks at each division, which is the challenge of decreasing landholding.
s: Child's share 0.75 hectare
Grandchild's share 0.25 hectare = 2,500 square metres
Concludes that holdings shrink with each division

questions.q: After untimely rain ruined his crop, Prakash borrowed money, could not repay it and is thinking of leaving farming. Which problem from the chapter is this?
questions.a: Loans taken in times of hardship that are hard to repay form the debt trap, which has led many farmers to abandon agriculture. The others are separate problems of the chapter.

Contamination of water and soil by pesticides
Division of land among heirs over generations
Dependence on seed companies for each year's seed

questions.q: Analyse the stress on the Ganga basin: say why the basin matters, list the causes of the stress the chapter gives, describe its effect on farming and suggest one solution that follows from the causes.
questions.a: The basin has rich alluvial soil and for millennia has supplied food and water to over 500 million people. Causes: Himalayan glaciers melting at an unprecedented rate, much water diverted for irrigation, huge groundwater pumping by agriculture and industry, and hundreds of dams. Effect: parts of the river are no longer navigable in summer and agriculture in the basin may become less sustainable, threatening livelihoods and food production. A solution might be efficient irrigation to cut water use.
s: Importance of the basin: alluvial soil and over 500 million people
Causes: any three
Effect on agriculture and livelihoods
A solution consistent with the causes
